sections.h2: Which Trenton offices handle property tax?
sections.html:
Two city offices and one county board split the work. The Division of Tax bills and collects, the Tax Assessor values the property, and the Mercer County Board of Taxation hears assessment appeals. The city's own page tells taxpayers that the collector handles billing and collection only, so any question about the assessed value goes to the assessor.

  • Division of Tax (billing, payments, delinquent notices, the annual tax sale): 609-989-3070.
  • Tax Assessor (value, deductions, exemptions, appeal forms): 609-989-3083.
  • Mercer County Board of Taxation, McDade Administration Building, 640 South Broad Street, Room 317, Trenton: 609-989-6704.

The Division of Tax also keeps records and files the reports state law requires, and it prepares lists of properties for tax foreclosure.

sections.h2: What kind of city is Trenton for a home seller?
sections.html:
It is a compact capital city where renters outnumber owners. Trenton is the capital of New Jersey and the seat of Mercer County, and it served briefly as the capital of the United States, from November 1 to December 24, 1784. Its motto, "Trenton Makes, The World Takes," dates from an industrial past of iron, steel, rubber and pottery, though today the state government dominates the local economy.

The Census Bureau counted 90,871 residents in 2020 and estimates 91,506 for 2025, packed into 7.58 square miles of land. That works out to nearly 12,000 people per square mile. Trenton is the only New Jersey city served by three commuter rail systems, Amtrak, NJ Transit and SEPTA, and the Trenton Transit Center sits in the East Ward beside Trenton Central High School.

Wikipedia describes the East Ward as the smallest of the city's neighborhoods and the West Ward as home to its more suburban streets, with Downtown, Hanover/Academy and Mill Hill among the named areas. Value and housing type shift a good deal from one part of the city to the next, so a figure for Trenton as a whole is only a starting point.

A seller here is often dealing with a rowhouse or older single family home on a small lot, sometimes with a tenant inside. The Census shows why: only 37.9% of homes are owner-occupied.

sections.h2: When are Trenton property taxes due, and when do bills arrive?
sections.html:
Payments are due on the first of February, May, August and November, with a ten day grace period before taxes are delinquent. Trenton does not follow the July mailing pattern used by calendar year towns. The city mails bills twice a year.

  • Late June or early July: bills for the August and November quarters.
  • Late December or early January: bills for the February and May quarters.

The first-half bills are the preliminary ones, based on about half of the prior year's taxes. When the second-half bill is issued it uses the current year's rate, and the preliminary amount is subtracted from the full-year total. That is why the winter quarters can look different from the summer ones even when the assessment has not moved.

sections.h2: How much interest does Trenton charge on late taxes?
sections.html:
Interest runs at 8% a year on delinquent balances up to $1,500 and 18% on the part above $1,500, counted from the first day of the quarter once the grace period ends. The city cites N.J.S.A. 54:4-67 for these rates. Once a delinquency has used up the $1,500 tier, later delinquencies are charged at 18% until the account balance returns to zero.

A 6% penalty may also be added to a delinquency above $10,000 that is still open at the end of the fiscal year. The city accepts partial payments, subject to the same interest rules. If you need proof of payment, enclose a self-addressed stamped envelope with the stub, or rely on the canceled check as your receipt.

sections.h2: When can Trenton sell a lien on unpaid taxes?
sections.html:
A municipal tax bill or charge still unpaid on May 11 is open to the tax sale, provided the sale takes place before the fiscal year ends on June 30. The city cites N.J.S.A. 54:5-19. From May 11 until the sale, payments must be made by certified check, cash or money order.

The rule is the same every year, and the Division of Tax holds the sale annually. An owner who plans to sell with taxes behind should clear the balance or have the payoff figure ready before May 11, because a lien adds a separate redemption step to the closing.

sections.h2: How do you appeal a Trenton assessment?
sections.html:
Regular assessment appeals must be filed by April 1 each year, and added or omitted assessment appeals by December 1. File with the Mercer County Board of Taxation. If your assessment exceeds $1,000,000 you may file directly with the New Jersey Tax Court, and a decision from the county board can be taken to Tax Court within 45 days.

Mercer County's instructions say one copy of the petition goes to the board at 640 South Broad Street, with one copy each to the municipal assessor and the municipal clerk. The board does not accept faxes or emailed copies. Its appeal page also offers an appeal checklist, appeal reminders and a comparable sales analysis form, and a seller who has recent sale prices for similar homes nearby should attach them. The county's 2026 notice put the deadline at Wednesday, April 1, 2026, which has passed, so a new filing now would be for the next tax year. The state Division of Taxation adds that an owner must show the assessment is unreasonable against a market value standard.

sections.h2: What should a Trenton seller do about the tax bill?
sections.html:
Give the bill to the buyer. The city states that when a property is sold the bill should be handed to the new owner, and a charge may be imposed for a duplicate. Ask the Division of Tax for a statement of what is paid and what is open before the closing date, because delinquency interest accrues from the first day of the quarter.

Flood zone status is another item the city mentions: if your municipality qualifies for federal flood insurance, an owner who does not buy it can be denied federal disaster assistance. Information on whether a property lies in a flood zone comes from the Municipal Clerk, which is worth checking when you list a home near the Delaware River.

faqs.q: How do I contact the Trenton tax office?
faqs.a: Call the Division of Tax at 609-989-3070. Assessment and deduction questions go to the Assessor at 609-989-3083. The collector deals with billing and collection only.

faqs.q: What is the grace period for Trenton property tax?
faqs.a: Ten days after the first of February, May, August or November. After that, taxes are delinquent and interest is counted from the first day of the quarter.

faqs.q: When is the Trenton tax appeal deadline?
faqs.a: April 1 for regular assessments and December 1 for added or omitted assessments. Appeals go to the Mercer County Board of Taxation, or to Tax Court if the assessment is over $1,000,000.

faqs.q: Why do my first-half and second-half Trenton bills differ?
faqs.a: The first-half bill is a preliminary amount based on about half of last year's taxes. The second-half bill uses the new rate for the year and subtracts the preliminary amount already billed.

faqs.q: Can Trenton sell a lien if I have owed tax for a long time?
faqs.a: Yes. Any bill still unpaid on May 11 is open to the tax sale, which must take place before June 30. Payments after May 11 require certified funds, cash or a money order.
